wine.name: Anna de Codorníu Blanc de Blancs
wine.grapes: Chardonnay, the larger part, with the three Catalan grapes of Cava: Parellada, Xarel·lo and Macabeo.
wine.sites: No single vineyard: a blend of white grapes for the Cava denomination, made and aged in the house's underground cellars at Sant Sadurní d'Anoia.
wine.making: Each grape is made into a still base wine; the blend is then bottled with sugar and yeast for its second fermentation in the bottle, the traditional method. The bottles rest on their lees in the cellars beneath Sant Sadurní for more than fifteen months, as the house's own page gives it, before disgorging and a Brut dosage.
wine.glass: Lemon peel, pear and green apple with a touch of dried pineapple, then a biscuity, lightly toasted finish from its time on the lees; a fine, gentle mousse and fresh, dry acidity.
wine.ageing: Ready on release and made to drink within a year or two, before its lemon and pear fade; the house keeps its long aged Cavas for other names.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a tulip or a white wine glass rather than a coupe, as an aperitif.

label.means: Named for the Codorníu heiress whose marriage in 1659 joined her family's vineyards to the Raventós family.
Made from white grapes only: here Chardonnay with the Catalan grapes, not Chardonnay alone.
Dry: less than twelve grams of sugar a litre after disgorging.
The denomination of traditional method sparkling wine, defined by its method and registered vineyards rather than one place.

records.table: A Codorníu heiress of the seventeenth century gave her name to Anna de Codorníu, the Chardonnay led Cava of the Sant Sadurní house where Cava began in 1872. This Blanc de Blancs brings lemon, pear and a biscuity finish, poured as an aperitif.
records.story: The Codorníu family were making wine at Sant Sadurní d'Anoia by 1551, when a family record lists their presses, barrels and vats. In 1659 Anna, the Codorníu heiress, married into the Raventós family, and the vineyards passed to the Raventós line, which kept the Codorníu name for the house. In 1872 the head of the family, back from a journey to Champagne, made, as the house tells it, a sparkling wine fermented a second time in the bottle from the estate's own Macabeo, Xarel·lo and Parellada, and the house dates Cava from that year. His son took charge at his death in 1885 and launched the house on a large scale; between the 1890s and 1915 the modernist architect Josep Puig i Cadafalch (1867 to 1956) built new cellars on the estate, declared a national historic and artistic monument in 1976. In 1984, as the house dates it, Codorníu launched Anna de Codorníu, named for the heiress and, by its own account, the first Cava to include Chardonnay beside the Catalan grapes. In 2018 the American investment fund Carlyle bought a majority of the company from the family. What Chardonnay brought to Cava's blend can be tasted in Anna, made by the house where the wine began.

others.name: Anna de Codorníu Brut
others.note: The lighter Anna, aged about a year on its lees by the house's page.

others.name: Codorníu Ars Collecta
others.note: The house's long aged range, with vintage dated Gran Reserva Blanc de Blancs among its bottlings.

traps: Blanc de Blancs on Anna de Codorníu means white grapes only, not Chardonnay alone: Parellada, Xarel·lo and Macabeo join it.
Codorníu dates its winemaking to 1551 and Cava to 1872: the first is a family record of presses and vats, the second its first bottle fermented sparkling wine.
Raventós i Blanc, which left Cava in 2012, is a separate estate of the same Raventós family, not a brand of Codorníu.

cards.front: Anna de Codorníu: which grape leads the blend, and when was it launched?
cards.back: Chardonnay, with Parellada, Xarel·lo and Macabeo; the house dates its launch to 1984 and calls it the first Cava to include Chardonnay.

cards.front: Whose name does Codorníu's Anna carry, and what did her marriage of 1659 do?
cards.back: The Codorníu heiress Anna; her marriage into the Raventós family brought the Codorníu vineyards to the Raventós line.

questions.q: A guest reads Blanc de Blancs on a bottle of Anna de Codorníu and expects Chardonnay alone. What is in it?
opts: Chardonnay with Parellada, Xarel·lo and Macabeo
Chardonnay alone from one walled vineyard
Pinot Noir and Chardonnay pressed pale
Xarel·lo alone from old bush vines
questions.exp: Anna is a Blanc de Blancs because all its grapes are white: Chardonnay leads, with the three Catalan grapes. Pinot Noir is a red grape, so it could never make a Blanc de Blancs.

questions.q: Codorníu dates Cava to 1872 at Sant Sadurní d'Anoia. What did the head of the Raventós family do that year?
opts: Made a wine fermented again in its bottle
Planted Chardonnay beside the Catalan grapes
Commissioned modernist cellars for the estate
Founded the regulating council of Cava
questions.exp: In 1872, after a journey to Champagne, he made a sparkling wine with a second fermentation in the bottle from the estate's own grapes; the modernist cellars came later, under his son.

sources.title: Codorníu: Anna de Codorníu Blanc de Blancs Reserve
Diputació de Barcelona: heritage inventory, Caves Codorníu

report: Searches for this record: 10 of the group's share of 35 (the house's history and Anna pages twice, the 1872 maker and his dates three times, the cellars twice, the launch of Anna twice, the glass once), one more shared with Freixenet on the sales of 2018; no fetch tried.

The plan's note is answered: 1659 rests on the house's Espacio Anna page with Matthew Clark and Glass of Bubbly (glassofbubbly.com/?p=28083); 1984 on Matthew Clark and several merchants, with one outlier of 1981 (azureazure.com) and one of 1983 (tastingbook.com); the sale of a majority to Carlyle in 2018 on Alimarket (alimarket.es/alimentacion/noticia/272649) and Catalan News (catalannews.com/business/item/us-firm-carlyle-to-buy-majority-stakehold-in-codorniu-for-390m).

The maker of 1872 is described, not named: Josep Raventós i Fatjó is given 1824 to 1885 by Decanter and 1816 to 1885 by the Wein Plus glossary, so his birth is unsettled; his son's taking charge at his death in 1885 rests on the Real Academia de la Historia's biography of Manuel Raventós i Domènech (dbe.rah.es/biografias/26029) and the Gran Enciclopèdia Catalana, whose dates for the son were not read.

The cellars' years are 1895 to 1915 by Wikipedia and 1902 to 1915 by the Diputació's inventory, which also gives Puig i Cadafalch's dates and the decree 248/1976 of 9 January; the story says between the 1890s and 1915.

The label taught is the Blanc de Blancs, which the house's own shop calls Reserve and gives more than fifteen months on its lees; since 2022 a Reserva of DO Cava is a Cava de Guarda Superior of eighteen months and a vintage, so classification is left empty and Reserva is not taught as a label term until the checker settles what the current bottle reads.

The grapes are Chardonnay about seventy per cent with the Catalan three by merchants' sheets, and the house's page names the Catalan grapes with Chardonnay added; the sites are left general, since no source read says where the Chardonnay grows.

The glass rests on the IWSC's note (iwsc.net/results/detail/95977) with Delectable's (lemon peel, green apple) and a critic's note not cited for the critic's name in its address; the house's page gives 11.5 to 12 degrees for serving, which reads like a confusion with the strength, so the record keeps the Codex's 8 to 10.

The region record's producers line calls Anna the first Chardonnay Cava, where the house says the first Cava to include Chardonnay; the record follows the house. No swap proposed; no living person named.

changed: table: "Launched in 1984 and named for a Codorníu heiress" now "Named for a Codorníu heiress of the seventeenth century": the year rests on the house alone against Wikipedia's Cava article, which dates the first Chardonnay Cava to 1981, so the spoken line keeps only what is settled.

story: the Raventós line kept the Codorníu name "on its bottles" now "for the house", since there were no bottles of the house's wine to name in 1659; the grapes of 1872 hedged as the house tells it, as the house's own page on DO Cava's site gives them.
story: "In 1984 the house launched" now "In 1984, as the house dates it, Codorníu launched", for the same conflict of 1984 against 1981.
cards[0].back: "the house launched it in 1984 as, by its own account, the first Cava to include Chardonnay" now "the house dates its launch to 1984 and calls it the first Cava to include Chardonnay".
sources: Grupo Raventós Codorníu's own history page (primary, read through search, 1984 and the first Chardonnay Cava as the house's claim) in place of Matthew Clark, a trade merchant's blog.
open: The first Chardonnay Cava: 1984 for Anna by the house's group page and the merchants; 1981 by Wikipedia's Cava article and one blog; one merchant says Chardonnay was authorised in Cava only in 1986. Both claims are hedged as the house's.

The label: importers' sheets and the house's shop give Blanc de Blancs Reserva with at least fifteen months on its lees, short of the eighteen a Reserva needs under the rules of 2020; whether the bottle of today still reads Reserva is unsettled, so classification stays empty and Reserva is not taught.
The cellars began in 1895 by Wikipedia, Arquitectura Catalana and Can Robira, in 1902 by the Diputació's inventory; the story keeps the 1890s.
The maker of 1872 stays unnamed: his birth year is 1816 or 1824 by the author's two sources, and no third was found.

wine.name: Freixenet Cordon Negro Brut
wine.grapes: Parellada, Macabeo and Xarel·lo, the three Catalan grapes of Cava.
wine.sites: Vineyards of the Penedès, by the house's account, blended and bottled at its cellars in Sant Sadurní d'Anoia.
wine.making: Made by the traditional method: the blended base wine takes sugar and yeast in its own bottle, ferments there a second time and rests on its lees for at least nine months, a year by the house's Spanish page; at disgorging it receives a Brut dosage of about nine grams a litre.
wine.glass: Apple and ripe pear with a lemony edge and a touch of ginger on a long finish; light, fresh and dry, made for drinking young.
wine.ageing: Drink it within a year or so of release, while its apple and pear are fresh; it is not a Cava for the cellar.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius, as the house advises; no need to decant; a flute or a tulip, as an aperitif or with fried food.

label.means: The house's Brut Cava in a frosted black bottle, launched in 1974.
Dry: less than twelve grams of sugar a litre; the house gives about nine.
Traditional method sparkling wine of the Cava denomination, fermented a second time in its own bottle.

records.table: The frosted black bottle that Freixenet, the Sant Sadurní house of the Ferrer and Sala families, launched in 1974 holds Cordon Negro Brut, a Cava of Parellada, Macabeo and Xarel·lo. Apple, pear and a touch of ginger make it a cold glass for anything fried.
records.story: Freixenet tells its history from two families. The Sala family's wine house, Casa Sala, was founded in 1861. A daughter of that family married a son of La Freixeneda, a Ferrer family estate in the Alt Penedès, and in 1914 the couple began to make Cava at Sant Sadurní d'Anoia; the name drawn from the Ferrer estate became the brand. The Civil War of 1936 to 1939 took the co-founder's husband and a son, killed in its first months, and she and her daughters kept the house going. A younger son later took the lead, and under him Freixenet launched Cordon Negro in 1974, a Brut of the three Catalan grapes in a frosted black bottle. It became the house's flagship and carried Freixenet's name abroad. In 2018 the German sparkling wine house Henkell took a majority of the company, and the two were joined as Henkell Freixenet. Freixenet stayed within DO Cava when the Corpinnat houses left it in 2019. Cordon Negro is often the first Cava a guest has met: the plain Brut of the Catalan grapes, made by the traditional method at scale.

others.name: Freixenet Carta Nevada
others.note: The house's older Cava brand, sold in a frosted white bottle.

others.name: Freixenet Cordon Negro Extra Dry
others.note: The off-dry sister of the Brut: Extra Dry on a sparkling label is sweeter than Brut.

others.name: Freixenet Cuvée D.S.
others.note: A cuvée the house named in honour of its co-founder of the Sala family.

traps: Extra Dry on a Cordon Negro label means off-dry, sweeter than the Brut, as Seco does on any Cava.
Cordon Negro is Cava, with its second fermentation in the bottle, not a tank method sparkling wine like most Prosecco.
Freixenet stayed within DO Cava; Gramona and Recaredo are among the Corpinnat houses that left it in 2019.

cards.front: Freixenet's Cordon Negro: what bottle is it known by, and when was it launched?
cards.back: A frosted black bottle; the house launched it in 1974.

cards.front: Which two families joined to found Freixenet at Sant Sadurní in 1914?
cards.back: The Sala family, whose wine house dates from 1861, and the Ferrer family of the La Freixeneda estate, which gave the brand its name.

questions.q: A guest asks what grapes make Freixenet's Cordon Negro Brut. Which answer is right?
questions.exp: Cordon Negro is a Cava of the three Catalan white grapes; Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier are Champagne's, Glera is Prosecco's, and the three reds are kept for rosado.

questions.q: Freixenet launched its Cordon Negro Brut in a frosted black bottle. In which decade did it reach the market?
questions.exp: Cordon Negro was launched in 1974, sixty years after the house first made Cava in 1914; the 1910s are the founding, not the black bottle.

sources.title: Grupo Freixenet: Cordón Negro, 50 years of the most universal Cava
Glass of Bubbly: major financial operations in Cava

report: Searches for this record: 5 of the group's share of 35 (the house's history twice, Cordon Negro's launch once, its sheet once, its glass once), one more shared with Codorníu on the sales of 2018; no fetch tried.

The plan's note is answered: 1914 and Casa Sala of 1861 rest on the house's own history, with the La Freixeneda estate and the families on its company blog; 1974 rests on the group's own page, the Henkell Freixenet newsroom (henkell-freixenet.com/en/news/newsroom/detail/celebrate-in-style-50-years-freixenet-cordon-negro-cava.html), Vinetur and Wine Industry Advisor; Henkell's majority of 2018 on Glass of Bubbly and Ara (en.ara.cat).

The founders are described, not named, for want of their dates: the house's pages give the couple as Dolors Sala Vivé and Pere Ferrer Bosch, and the son who led the house from 1957 and launched Cordon Negro is not named, since I could not confirm whether he is living; the house's German press kit adds his nephew as co-author of the launch, one source only and a living man, left out.

Left out for want of a second independent source: the founder and a son killed in the Civil War (the International Directory of Company Histories, mirrored by Funding Universe and Encyclopedia.com, one text); Carta Nevada's launch, 1941 on the house's history page and most merchants but 1927 on the house's own timeline, with the frosted white bottle of 1966 in the German press kit; the claim of the first imported sparkling wine in the United States in 1983, the house's alone.

The lees time is nine months on the house's American and global pages and at least twelve on its Spanish and German pages; the record gives both. The serving temperature, 6 to 8 degrees, is the house's and the Codex region record's for a Cava Brut, below the brief's general 8 to 10 for sparkling.
The respelling is the author's from the Catalan (x as sh), which no source read gives; the checker may prefer fresh-uh-NET.
Not in WINE_PRODUCERS; no swap proposed. Living names met, none in the fragment: the son and nephew of the founding family named by the press kit.

changed: story: La Freixeneda "whose history reaches back to the thirteenth century" cut: the house's own account gives the thirteenth century and the International Directory of Company Histories has the Ferrer family establish the estate in the sixteenth.

story: "struck the house hard, and after it the co-founder and her eldest daughter took charge and set the house working again" now "took the co-founder's husband and a son, killed in its first months, and she and her daughters kept the house going": the International Directory, Spanish Wikipedia and the obituaries of 2024 tell the killings and a mother and daughters who kept the house; none read gives the eldest daughter alone.

story: "Their son became head of the house in 1957" now "A younger son later took the lead": 1957 is the International Directory's, while Spanish Wikipedia and the obituaries give his joining in 1947, the general management in 1959 and the presidency in 1978.
sources: Spanish Wikipedia's José Ferrer Sala in place of Vinetur, whose year 1974 the house's own page already carries.
open: The son who led the house died on 5 November 2024 aged 99 by the house's own obituary and three trade papers; he is not living and may be named with his dates once his birth year is read in two sources.

Henkell's share of 2018: a majority by the author's sources and two of the refuter's, an equal structure at first by one; one site of 2026 reports that Henkell bought the remaining half in March 2026, one source only and not told.
Carta Nevada's year (1927 or 1941) and the year of its frosted white bottle were not tested; the record gives no year.
The respelling freh-sheh-NET stays: Catalan reads the x as sh, and no source read offers one.

wine.name: Gramona III Lustros Brut Nature
wine.grapes: Xarel·lo leading, with Macabeo, and Parellada in some recent years; the blend shifts with the vintage.
wine.sites: La Plana, the family's estate in the Anoia valley at Sant Sadurní d'Anoia, on the ground called Font de Jui, farmed organically on biodynamic lines by the house's account.
wine.making: A vintage wine. The base wine is bottled for its second fermentation under a natural cork stopper rather than a crown cap, which the house keeps for wines aged more than five years, and it rests on its lees in the cellars for more than eighty months. It is disgorged with no sugar added: Brut Nature.
wine.glass: Brioche and bread dough over chamomile, dried apricot and toasted almond, with candied lemon peel and a hint of aniseed; creamy in texture yet very dry, with fresh acidity and a long, dry finish.
wine.ageing: Released after some seven years on its lees and ready to drink then; a cool cellar keeps it for a few years more as it grows nuttier.
wine.serve: 9 to 11 degrees Celsius, never ice cold; no need to decant; a white wine glass rather than a flute, at the table.

label.means: Three lustra, three spans of five years: a name for the long ageing the wine was made to show.
No sugar added at disgorging, under three grams a litre.
The collective mark of Penedès houses that left DO Cava in 2019: organic grapes, hand picked, at least eighteen months on lees.
The Cava rank on bottles labelled before 2019: at least thirty months on the lees.

records.table: More than seven years on its lees under natural cork shape III Lustros, Gramona's Xarel·lo led sparkling wine from the family's La Plana estate, disgorged with no sugar added. Toasty, nutty and very dry, it is poured with food, in a white wine glass.
records.story: The house's name came by marriage. In 1921 the daughter of a winemaking family and her husband, a Gramona and a son of the president of the Barcelona taverners' guild, began to make sparkling wine, and the house took his name. Her family's line in wine reached back to around 1850, to a grower and winemaker who worked the La Plana vineyards in the Anoia valley for the family that owned them; his son, her father, opened the family's first cellar in 1881 and later bought La Plana itself. The couple's children laid down the first III Lustros in 1951, as the house tells it to prove that a sparkling wine could age for years on its lees, and released it in 1961; the name, three spans of five years, speaks of that patience. The house kept its long aged wines under natural cork for the second fermentation and turned the La Plana estate to organic farming on biodynamic lines. In 2019 Gramona was among the founding houses of Corpinnat that left DO Cava, wanting stricter rules on organic grapes, hand picking and making on the estate, so later releases carry Corpinnat where older ones read Cava Gran Reserva. Xarel·lo, given years on its lees, is the grape III Lustros was made to show.

others.name: Gramona Celler Batlle
others.note: Named for the Batlle family of the first cellar, from the first vineyard the family owned, and held on its lees for longer.

others.name: Gramona Enoteca
others.note: Late releases of the long aged wines, disgorged after many more years in the cellar.

traps: Corpinnat is a collective mark outside DO Cava, not a tier of Cava: III Lustros bottles from before 2019 say Cava, later ones Corpinnat.
III Lustros means three spans of five years, a name for long ageing; the wine rests some seven years on its lees, not fifteen.
Gramona ages its long wines under natural cork, not a crown cap, during the second fermentation.

cards.front: Gramona III Lustros: how is the bottle closed while it rests on its lees, and for how long?
cards.back: Under a natural cork stopper rather than a crown cap, for more than eighty months, some seven years.

cards.front: When did Gramona lay down its first III Lustros, and when was it released?
cards.back: The first tirage was in 1951; the wine reached the market in 1961.

questions.q: During its years on the lees, how is a bottle of Gramona III Lustros sealed?
opts: With a plastic stopper and wire
questions.exp: The house keeps natural cork for wines aged more than five years, saying it lets in the little oxygen the yeast needs; a crown cap is the usual closure for a shorter second fermentation.

questions.q: Gramona's first III Lustros was laid down in 1951. What did the family set out to show with it?
opts: That a sparkling wine could age for years
That Chardonnay could replace the Catalan grapes
That Cava could be made by the tank method
That the Penedès could ripen Cabernet Sauvignon
questions.exp: As the house tells it, III Lustros was made to prove that long ageing on the lees was possible, with Xarel·lo the grape that allows it; Chardonnay plays no part in the wine.

sources.title: Decanter: Nine Spanish producers to quit Cava DO

report: Searches for this record: 5 of the group's share of 35 (the house's history twice, III Lustros's pages twice, its glass once), one more shared with Recaredo on Corpinnat; no fetch tried.

The plan's note is answered: the house's page gives more than eighty months under natural cork and its sheet more than eighty four, so the record says more than eighty, some seven years; the label read Cava Gran Reserva Brut Nature on older bottles (Vinissimus, Bodeboca) and Corpinnat Brut Nature since 2019 by the house and merchants; one merchant shows a 2017 labelled Reserva, which the checker may wish to test.

1850, 1881, 1921, 1951 and 1961 rest on the house's own history pages; the founders are described, not named, since no dates were found for Josep Batlle, Pau Batlle, Pilar Batlle or Bartomeu Gramona, and the brothers of the 1950s are named by no page read.

The blend shifts: Xarel·lo seventy and Macabeo thirty by European Cellars, seventy five and twenty five for the 2010, and forty one Xarel·lo, thirty nine Macabeo and twenty Parellada on the house's current sheet; the library's Xarel·lo with Macabeo stands, with Parellada added for recent years.

Corpinnat's founding and the exit of 2019 rest on Decanter, Vinex (en.vinex.market, 4 February 2019), Catalonia Today and Recaredo's and Corpinnat's own pages; the rules (organic, hand picked, eighteen months) on the Wine Scholar Guild and Decanter, and they agree with the Codex region record.

The glass rests on Spanish Wine Lover's notes of the 2007, 2009 and 2011 (toast, aniseed, ripe citrus, creamy) with notes of the 2006 (brioche, bread dough, almond) and of a later bottling (hazelnut, almond); hand disgorging, which the library does not claim, was found on no page and is not said.

Left out: the house's claim that III Lustros was the first long aged Spanish sparkling wine (one source, the house); the size of La Plana (volatile). No swap proposed; living names met, none in the fragment: the family's present heads named in Corpinnat's news.

changed: wine.glass: hazelnut out, chamomile and dried apricot in, from the house's own III Lustros sheet (white fruit, chamomile, brioche, breadcrumbs, dried apricot), beside the critics' brioche, bread dough, almond, candied citrus and aniseed the author read.
open: The first release: 1961 by the house and most accounts, 1959 by one; the record keeps 1961.

The words on bottles since 2019: Corpinnat Brut Nature by the house, while merchants list a 2017 as Reserva and others as Gran Reserva; the record teaches Gran Reserva only for bottles labelled before 2019.
The serve, 9 to 11 degrees Celsius, is within the Codex's range for a fuller sparkling wine; no figure for III Lustros was found on the house's sheets.

wine.name: Turó d'en Mota de Recaredo Brut Nature
wine.sites: Turó d'en Mota, a small plot of bush vines planted in 1940 on a calcareous hillside at Sant Sadurní d'Anoia, dry farmed on biodynamic lines.
wine.making: Picked by hand, the Xarel·lo of the one plot makes a vintage wine whose second fermentation takes place under a natural cork stopper. It rests more than a hundred months on its lees, ten years and more in recent releases, and every bottle is disgorged by hand, by the house's account without freezing the neck, with no sugar added.
wine.glass: Chamomile, honey and dried white flowers over candied tangerine zest, white peach and hazelnut, with a touch of meadow herbs; firm and very dry, held by fresh acidity, with a long finish.
wine.ageing: A decade or so on its lees comes before release, and it is ready then; the house's late Enoteca releases of the 1999 and 2001 show it can go on for many years more.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius, as the house advises, the bottle opened a few minutes before; no need to decant; a white wine glass, never a flute, with food at the table.

label.means: The name of the single plot; turó is Catalan for a small hill.
No sugar added at disgorging; the house makes vintage Brut Nature alone, by its own account.
The collective mark of the Penedès houses that left DO Cava in 2019, which Recaredo helped to found.

records.table: One hillside plot at Sant Sadurní makes Recaredo's Turó d'en Mota: Xarel·lo alone from bush vines planted in 1940, aged more than a hundred months under cork and disgorged by hand with no sugar added. Lightly chilled, it is opened for the meal, not the toast.
records.story: The founder began in sparkling wine in 1924 as a disgorger at Sant Sadurní d'Anoia, and with pick and spade he dug a cellar beneath his own house in the old centre of the town, as the family tells it; the house carries his father's first name. The family kept to dry farming and in time turned to biodynamics, certified by Demeter, and to vintage wines of Brut Nature alone, every bottle aged under natural cork and disgorged by hand. Turó d'en Mota, a small hillside plot of Xarel·lo bush vines planted in 1940, was first picked on its own in 1999. That wine stayed on its lees until 2008, when the house released it as, by its own account, the first Penedès sparkling wine of Xarel·lo alone from a single vineyard. Recaredo helped to found Corpinnat in 2019, leaving DO Cava with the other founding houses, and its labels gave up the word Cava for the collective mark. Its later Enoteca releases of the 1999 and 2001 have shown how long the wine can rest. Turó d'en Mota asks a guest to taste one hillside, and the years its wine spent in the cellar.

others.name: Recaredo Terrers
others.note: A vintage Brut Nature of the house, aged for years under natural cork and disgorged by hand.

others.name: Reserva Particular de Recaredo
others.note: A vintage Brut Nature of the house, sold under the Corpinnat mark.

others.name: Enoteca Turó d'en Mota
others.note: Late releases of old vintages of Turó d'en Mota, such as the 1999 and 2001.

traps: Turó d'en Mota names the vineyard, not the house: the producer is Recaredo, a name taken from the founder's father.
Older bottles of Turó d'en Mota read Cava Brut Nature Gran Reserva; later ones carry Corpinnat, since the house left DO Cava in 2019.
Brut Nature on Recaredo means no sugar at all is added at disgorging; Extra Brut would allow a little.

cards.front: Recaredo's Turó d'en Mota: what grape, and from vines planted when?
cards.back: Xarel·lo alone, from bush vines planted in 1940 on a calcareous hillside at Sant Sadurní d'Anoia.

cards.front: How does Recaredo disgorge its bottles, and what sugar does it add?
cards.back: By hand after ageing under natural cork, by its own account without freezing the neck; it adds none, making Brut Nature alone.

questions.q: Recaredo's Turó d'en Mota comes from one hillside plot at Sant Sadurní. Which grape grows there?
questions.exp: Turó d'en Mota is Xarel·lo alone from bush vines planted in 1940; Macabeo and Parellada are the other Catalan grapes of Cava, and Chardonnay has no part in this wine.

questions.q: Recaredo picked Turó d'en Mota on its own for the first time in 1999. When did that wine reach the market?
questions.exp: The 1999 rested on its lees for some nine years until the house released it in 2008; 2019 is the year Recaredo left DO Cava for Corpinnat.

sources.title: Recaredo: Enoteca 1999 de Turó d'en Mota
Corpinnat: the first bottles under the collective brand name
Decanter: Wine Legend, Recaredo Turó d'en Mota 1999

report: Searches for this record: 5 of the group's share of 35 (the house's history once, the vineyard's sheets once, the cellar's methods once, the glass once, the year it left Cava once), one more shared with Gramona on Corpinnat; no fetch tried.

The plan's note is answered: 1924, the founder's start as a disgorger and the cellar dug beneath his house rest on the house's Origins page; the planting of 1940 on the house's Turó d'en Mota page and Mentta's technical sheet (mentta.com); the first harvest of 1999 and the release of spring 2008 on the house's pages, with Spanish Wine Lover's Turó d'en Mota, ageing gracefully since 1999.
The founder and his father are described, not named: the house gives them as Josep Mata Capellades and Recaredo Mata Figueres, and no dates were found for either.

The lees time is more than a hundred months on the house's page, 120 months for the 2010 and 150 for the 2012 by the sheets; the record says more than a hundred months, ten years and more in recent releases. No source read says whether the base wine sees oak, so the record does not say.

Corpinnat: Recaredo is among the founding houses by its own page and Corpinnat's, and the exit of February 2019 rests on Decanter, Vinex and Catalonia Today; one GuildSomm article is reported to say Recaredo left in 2015 and one merchant 2018, both against the rest, and are not followed. Demeter is on the house's labels as read through its shop; the year of certification was not found and is not given.

The glass rests on Spanish Wine Lover's note of the 2005 (chamomile, honey, withered flowers, firm acidity), Falstaff's of the 2003 (candied tangerine zest, white peach, meadow herbs) and a merchant's (hazelnut); the serving temperature is the Codex's for a fuller sparkling wine.
Not in WINE_PRODUCERS; no swap proposed. Living names met, none in the fragment: the family's present head, Corpinnat's president, named by Catalonia Today and the house's press pages.

changed: wine.making: "disgorged by hand without freezing the neck" now "disgorged by hand, by the house's account without freezing the neck": the house and Rosenthal say so, while Decanter's Wine Legend says the 1999 was disgorged by hand after the neck was frozen.

wine.serve: "10 to 12 degrees Celsius" now "8 to 10 degrees Celsius, as the house advises, the bottle opened a few minutes before", by the house's Turó d'en Mota page (its shop gives 10), and in the Codex's range for sparkling wine.

story: "certified by Demeter as its labels state" now "certified by Demeter" (merchants give the certification; no label was read), and the freezing of the neck cut from the story for the conflict above.
story: "until the spring of 2008" now "until 2008": spring by the house, October 2008 by Decanter's Wine Legend.
story: "gave up the words Cava and Gran Reserva on its labels" now "its labels gave up the word Cava": one importer still names the wine Corpinnat Gran Reserva, so the second word is not settled.
questions[1].opts: seasons and years ("In the spring of 2008") now four years (In 2008, In 2000, In 2002, In 2019), since the season is in dispute; the explanation adds the nine years on the lees.
cards[1].back: the freezing of the neck hedged as the house's own account.

others[0]: Terrers "aged at least fifty months under natural cork by its label" now "aged for years under natural cork and disgorged by hand": one article gives 52 months at a last disgorging and no label was read.

sources: Decanter's Wine Legend of the 1999 (the planting of 1940, the first single vineyard Cava, the release of 2008) in place of Catalonia Today, whose exit of 2019 Corpinnat's own page and the drinks press carry.
open: Disgorging without freezing: the house and Rosenthal against Decanter's account of the 1999; the record says it as the house's account.
Dry farming rests on the house's page and one encyclopaedia entry; the year of the Demeter certification (2010 by one account) is not given.
The house's claim that the 1999 was the first Penedès sparkling wine of Xarel·lo alone from one vineyard: Decanter calls it the first single vineyard Cava; kept as the house's account.

wine.name: Mas La Plana Cabernet Sauvignon
wine.sites: The Mas La Plana vineyard at Pacs del Penedès, planted with Cabernet Sauvignon in 1966 by the house's account, in ten plots on two levels of deep soils over alluvial gravels and silts.
wine.making: Macerated on its skins for two to three weeks and fermented under temperature control in stainless steel and oak vats, then aged about eighteen months in French oak barriques, much of it new, with a small share in large oak casks.
wine.glass: Cassis and black cherry over cocoa, coffee and a lift of menthol, with cedar from the oak; full and firm, with ripe, dense tannin and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Firm in its first years, it rewards a decade in bottle and lasts well beyond, as the house's releases of old vintages show.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; open a young bottle an hour or two ahead in a decanter, and pour an old one off its sediment with care; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The name of the vineyard at Pacs del Penedès, which the wine took in the 1990s.
The wine's older name, Etiqueta Negra in Spanish, under which the 1970 won in Paris in 1979.
The denomination of origin of the Penedès, chiefly for still wines; Cava is a separate denomination.

records.table: Sold as Gran Coronas Black Label, the 1970 of Familia Torres's Mas La Plana came first among the Cabernets at a Paris Wine Olympiad in 1979. One vineyard at Pacs grows the Cabernet Sauvignon, which spends about eighteen months in French oak; give it a decanter and red meat.
records.story: Two brothers founded the house at Vilafranca del Penedès in 1870 as a grower and exporter of wine, one of them back from Cuba with a fortune made there. In 1939, months before the end of the Civil War, the family's cellar was partly destroyed in a bombing raid on the town's railway station. Miguel Torres Carbó (1909 to 1991), of the third generation, rebuilt it and turned the house towards bottled wines under its own brands, Coronas and Sangre de Toro among them. In the 1960s the next generation, against the habits of the region, chose Cabernet Sauvignon for the family's Mas La Plana estate at Pacs del Penedès, planted in 1966, and the first vintage, the 1970, was sold as Gran Coronas Black Label. In 1979 that wine was placed first among the Cabernet Sauvignons at the Wine Olympiad held by Gault Millau in Paris, a result that drew notice abroad to Penedès red. In the 1990s the wine took the name of its vineyard. Because of Mas La Plana, a guest may know the Penedès for red wine as well as for Cava.

others.name: Gran Coronas
others.note: The house's older Penedès red, whose name the 1970 Black Label carried.

others.name: Milmanda
others.note: A barrel fermented Chardonnay of the family, from Conca de Barberà rather than the Penedès.

others.name: Grans Muralles
others.note: A red of recovered Catalan grapes from Conca de Barberà, not a Penedès wine.

traps: Mas La Plana is a Penedès Cabernet Sauvignon; Grans Muralles and Milmanda, also the family's, come from Conca de Barberà.
The 1970 that came first in Paris was not Cabernet alone: it was mostly Cabernet Sauvignon with some Tempranillo and Monastrell, where the Mas La Plana of the house's sheets is Cabernet alone.
The Paris result of 1979 was the Gault Millau Wine Olympiad, not the Judgement of Paris of 1976, which set Californian wines beside French ones.

cards.front: Familia Torres's Mas La Plana: what did its 1970 achieve, where and when?
cards.back: Sold as Gran Coronas Black Label, it came first among the Cabernet Sauvignons at Gault Millau's Wine Olympiad in Paris in 1979.

cards.front: What grape is Mas La Plana, and where is its vineyard?
cards.back: Cabernet Sauvignon alone, from the Mas La Plana vineyard at Pacs del Penedès, planted in 1966.

questions.q: A guest asks how Torres ages Mas La Plana before release. Which answer fits?
opts: About eighteen months in French oak barriques
About six years in old American oak
A year in steel tanks, then concrete
Three years in large chestnut casks
questions.exp: The house ages it about eighteen months, nearly all in French oak barriques and much of it new; long years in old American oak belong to traditional Rioja, not to this Cabernet.

questions.q: In 1979 a Torres Cabernet of the 1970 vintage came first in its class at a tasting in Paris. Under what name was it sold?
questions.exp: The 1970 was sold as Gran Coronas Black Label, Etiqueta Negra in Spanish; the wine took the vineyard's name, Mas La Plana, only in the 1990s.

sources.title: Familia Torres: Mas La Plana 2020 technical sheet
Decanter: Wine Legend, Torres Gran Coronas Reserva Cabernet Sauvignon 1970

report: Searches for this record: 5 of the group's share of 35 (the wine's history once, its ageing and change of name once, the house's history once, its technical sheet once, its glass once); no fetch tried.

The plan's note is answered: the 1970 as Gran Coronas Etiqueta Negra and the Gault Millau Olympiad of 1979 rest on the house's Mas La Plana page and Decanter's Wine Legend; the change of name is from the 1995 vintage by Decanter and the early 1990s by Squelch, so the record says the 1990s.

1870 and the two brothers rest on the house's history; the brother back from Cuba is described, not named, since the house gives his dates as 1843 to 1904 and a paper of the Institut d'Estudis Catalans (publicacions.iec.cat) as 1839 to 1906; Miguel Torres Carbó's dates, 1909 to 1991, are the house's own, read through search, and the bombing of 1939 is the house's account.

The planting of 1966 is on several of the house's pages and one other house page says the 1970s; the record keeps 1966 as the house's account. The man who chose Cabernet is living and is said as the next generation; the house's early vintages are said by one merchant to have held some Tempranillo before 1978, left out.

The making rests on the 2020 sheet (fifteen to twenty five days on the skins, steel and oak vats, eighteen months, nearly all in barriques, about two thirds new, the rest in casks of 30 hectolitres); the glass on Falstaff's note of the 2016 (cocoa bean, menthol, blackcurrant), Decanter's as quoted by Farr Vintners (cassis, cherry, cedar), the house's (chocolate, coffee, ripe tannin) and Wilson Daniels' (firm tannin).

The library's why says the 1970 beat first growths, and its note on Mas La Plana the same; the house says it beat the most acclaimed Cabernets, so the record says only that it came first among the Cabernet Sauvignons, and the library line is for the checker to test. Milmanda and Grans Muralles rest on the library alone and are taught as it teaches them.
The house's base is Pacs del Penedès by the library and the founding was at Vilafranca by the house; the record keeps both. No swap proposed; no living person named.

changed: story: "a fortune made in shipping and trade" now "a fortune made there": the accounts read differ on what he did in Cuba (a store in Havana, a partnership of 1865).

story: "the family's cellar was destroyed in the bombing aimed at the town's railway station" now "partly destroyed in a bombing raid on the town's railway station": one timeline gives partly destroyed, another a good part of the neighbouring wineries razed.
story: "bottling its wines under the family's name for sale abroad" now "bottled wines under its own brands, Coronas and Sangre de Toro among them", by the Gran Enciclopèdia Catalana.
story: "In the late 1960s" now "In the 1960s", since the planting was in 1966 (1964 by one account).

traps[1]: the old names trap, already taught by the label and the story question, replaced by the 1970's blend: about seventy per cent Cabernet Sauvignon with Tempranillo and Monastrell by Decanter's Wine Legend and Vintage Wine and Port's listing, where the house's sheets give Cabernet alone.
sources: the Gran Enciclopèdia Catalana (Miguel Torres Carbó's dates and brands) in place of Squelch.
open: The vintage from which Mas La Plana became Cabernet Sauvignon alone: one merchant says from 1978; not settled.
The planting: 1966 by the house and most accounts, 1964 by one.
The change of name: the 1995 vintage by Decanter and one more account, the early 1990s by Squelch; the record says the 1990s.
